extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (real & complex analysis) / contest-oriented readers
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook material defining and proving criteria for extending uniformly continuous functions, defining the Riemann integral (via rectangle functions and tagged partitions), and introducing basic complex-analysis notions (holomorphic functions, contour integrals, Cauchy theorems and consequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dense set (Definition 30.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let S be a subset (or subspace) of a topological space X. Then S is dense if every open subset of X contains a point of S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Q is dense in R; any metric space M is dense in its completion. Dense subspaces allow unique extensions of continuous/uniformly continuous maps by approximation of points by sequences from S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of uniformly continuous functions (Theorem 30.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let M be a metric space, N a complete metric space, and S a dense subspace of M. If ψ : S → N is uniformly continuous, then there exists a unique continuous extension eψ : M → N making the inclusion commute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof outline: approximate each x∈M by a sequence in S; uniform continuity makes ψ(x_n) Cauchy; completeness of N gives a limit which defines eψ(x); uniqueness follows because limits of approximating sequences are forced to agree. Exercise: show ψ(x_n) is Cauchy using uniform continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure modes for extensions (Example 30.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two ways extension from a dense subset S to closure M can fail: (a) target N is not complete, so the limit of ψ(x_n) may not exist in N; (b) ψ may 'explode' near limit points of S so no finite limit exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (a) identity Q→Q cannot extend to R→Q because Q is not complete; (b) f(x)=1/√(x−√2) on Q has blow-up near √2, preventing extension to R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectangle functions R([a,b]) and M([a,b]) (Definition 30.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: R([a,b]) denotes functions constant on a finite partition's subintervals [t0,t1),[t1,t2),...,[tn−1,tn] with convention left-closed/right-open except last which is closed. C0([a,b]) is continuous functions; M([a,b]) = C0([a,b]) ∪ R([a,b]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rectangular step functions are the elementary objects whose summed areas define the integral on the dense subset; note the chosen endpoint convention (left endpoint closed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremum metric on M([a,b]) (Definition 30.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define d(f,g) = sup_{x∈[a,b]} |f(x) − g(x)| on M([a,b]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This metric (uniform/sup norm) is used to state density, continuity, and to apply completion/extension arguments (uniform continuity in this metric gives control over integrals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectangle-sum map Σ: R([a,b]) → R (definition and uniform continuity)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a rectangle function constant values f(t_i) on each piece, Σ(f) is the sum of areas f(t0)(t1−a) + f(t1)(t2−t1)+...+f(tn)(b−tn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Σ is uniformly continuous in the sup metric: if d(f,g)<ε then |Σ(f)−Σ(g)| < ε(b−a). This uniform continuity is a hypothesis needed to extend Σ to continuous functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and uniqueness of the Riemann integral via extension (Theorem 30.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a unique continuous map R_a^b : M([a,b]) → R extending Σ (i.e., making the diagram with inclusion of R([a,b]) commute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the extension theorem: need R([a,b]) dense in M([a,b]), Σ uniformly continuous, and R complete. Thus every continuous function has a well-defined Riemann integral defined by this continuous extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density of rectangle functions in continuous functions (proof idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: R([a,b]) is dense in M([a,b]): for any continuous f and ε>0 there exists a rectangle function approximating f within ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument uses uniform continuity of f: choose δ so intervals have width <δ and pick rectangle heights from points on graph (upper-left corner convention) to get sup-norm closeness <ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tagged partition and mesh (Definition 30.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tagged partition P of [a,b] is a partition a=t0<...<tn=b together with sample points ξ_i ∈ [t_{i−1},t_i]. The mesh of P is max_i (t_i − t_{i−1}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tagged partitions encode the usual Riemann-sum sampling scheme; tags ξ_i are the sampling points used in Riemann sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann integral as limit of Riemann sums (Theorem 30.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : [a,b] → R is continuous, then ∫_a^b f(x) dx equals the limit of Σ_{i=1}^n f(ξ_i)(t_i−t_{i−1}) as the mesh of tagged partitions → 0 (the limit is independent of the particular sequence of tagged partitions whose mesh → 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: interpret each Riemann sum as Σ of an approximating rectangle function g_n with mesh→0; uniform continuity implies d(f,g_n)→0, then continuity of the extension Σ gives convergence of Σ(g_n) to R(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Riemann integrability for general functions (Definition 30.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A (not necessarily continuous) function f : [a,b] → R is Riemann integrable if the limit of Riemann sums over tagged partitions exists as mesh→0; the integral is that limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment: many such functions are integrable (piecewise continuous, continuous a.e.); later the text notes every Riemann integrable function is Lebesgue integrable and Lebesgue theory is more powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical computation and Fundamental Theorem remark (Example 30.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is an antiderivative of f (continuous derivative etc.), then ∫_a^b f = F(b)−F(a); antiderivatives are unique up to additive constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ∫_1^4 x^2 dx = (1/3)x^3|_1^4 = 21. Also remark on the common notation ∫ x^2 dx = (1/3)x^3 + C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex derivative and holomorphic functions (§31.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f:U→C, the complex derivative at z0 is lim_{h→0} (f(z0+h)−f(z0))/h (complex limit). f is holomorphic if differentiable at all points of its domain; entire if on C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex differentiability is stronger than real differentiability because h can approach 0 from any direction in the plane. Topological viewpoint: requires U open so δ-neighborhoods exist.

rubrics_metrics.description:

 h/h does not have a unique limit as h→0 from different directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a counterexample to show that simple-looking maps may fail holomorphicity; check directional limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic closedness properties of holomorphic functions (Example 31.2.2(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Sums, products, nonzero quotients, compositions of holomorphic functions are holomorphic; standard elementary holomorphic examples include polynomials, exp, sin, cos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for building new holomorphic functions from known ones; derivatives follow the same rules as in real calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contour integral definition (§31.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a path α:[a,b]→C (contour), define ∫_α f(z) dz = ∫_a^b f(α(t)) α'(t) dt. The value depends only on the geometric path not parametrization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paths should be continuous and piecewise differentiable (allow finitely many 'sharp bends' but bounded length). Reparametrizations of the same geometric curve give the same contour integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral of z^m around unit circle (Theorem 31.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the unit circle γ(t)=e^{it}, ∮_γ z^m dz = 2πi if m = −1, and 0 otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a basic computational fact used repeatedly (connects to residues). Intuitive symmetry argument for m≥0 yields cancellation; direct computation via parametrization shows the m=−1 case yields 2πi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy-Goursat theorem (Theorem 31.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Ω is open and simply connected and f:Ω→C is holomorphic, then the integral of f around any loop γ in Ω is 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanity check: functions with singularities (like 1/z on C\{0}) can violate the conclusion because domain isn't simply connected. Classic proofs use Green's theorem under extra smoothness hypotheses or Goursat's approach for the general case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy integral formula (Theorem 31.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If γ is a circle bounding a disk D and f is holomorphic on a neighborhood containing γ and its interior, then for a in interior: f(a) = (1/2πi) ∮_γ f(z)/(z−a) dz.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses a keyhole contour around a and Cauchy-Goursat, then estimates the small circle integral via the ML lemma. This formula represents interior values by boundary integrals and is the basis for many consequences (power series, derivative formulas).

rubrics_metrics.name: M L estimation lemma (Lemma 31.5.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f continuous on a path α of length L and M = max_{z on α} |f(z)|, one has |∮_α f(z) dz| ≤ M·L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to show integrals over small loops tend to 0 as loop length→0; used in estimates in proofs (e.g., bounding the integral of (f(z)−f(a))/(z−a) over a small circle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Holomorphic implies analytic (Taylor series representation, §31.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is holomorphic on a disk D centered at p then f(z)=Σ_{k≥0} c_k (z−p)^k for z in D, with c_k = (1/2πi) ∮_γ f(w)/(w−p)^{k+1} dw = f^{(k)}(p)/k!. Holomorphic ⇒ infinitely differentiable and equal to its Taylor series on some disk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Cauchy integral formula, geometric series expansion, interchange of sum and integral (Weierstrass M-test). The radius of validity is limited by how large a disk centered at p stays inside the domain U.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy differentiation formula (Theorem 31.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f holomorphic on a disk D bounded by γ and center p, f^{(k)}(p) = k!/(2πi) ∮_γ f(w)/(w−p)^{k+1} dw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives explicit integral formulas for derivatives and underlies the fact holomorphic functions have power-series expansions with coefficients determined by contour integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences/problems illustrating power (Problems 31A–31F)
rubrics_metrics.description: Important consequences/applications: Liouville's theorem (bounded entire ⇒ constant), zeros are isolated unless f≡0 on open set, identity theorem (agree on neighborhood ⇒ equal on connected open set), maximum modulus principle (max of |f| on compact set occurs on boundary), Picard-type density of image of nonconstant entire functions, removable singularity theorem (bounded near puncture ⇒ removable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as problems but express standard criteria/consequences used to judge/understand holomorphic functions; they show how representation and integral formulas imply strong rigidity properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meromorphic function definition (§32.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A meromorphic function on U is a function expressible as A(z)/B(z) with A,B holomorphic on U and B not identically zero (poles allowed where B=0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prototype example: 1/z. Meromorphic functions generalize holomorphic ones by admitting isolated poles; residue calculus and argument principle (later) rely on this notion.
